li.a: SABH: Gudovac, scene of the first mass crime
SABH: On the massacre in Gudovac of 28 April 1941
Portal Novosti: Commemoration for the Serb victims in Gudovac
Portal Novosti: Let us keep the memory of the victims with dignity
VeDRA: The day the Ustaša dance of death began

content.p: On Monday 28 April 1941, armed men rounded up Serb villagers around Gudovac, a village near the town of Bjelovar in northern Croatia, marched them to a market meadow beside the Plavnica river and shot them in the dusk. Roughly 200 people were taken; the sources agree that all but a handful died. It happened 18 days after the Independent State of Croatia (NDH) was proclaimed, and commemoration groups and the Croatian antifascist veterans' association describe it as the first organised mass killing of Serbs in that state. The killers were arrested by German soldiers but soon released.
The exact toll has never been settled. Lists compiled over the following decades give 187, 192, 195, 196 or 201 names, and the argument over numbers is part of the story.

SABH, the Croatian association of antifascist fighters, traces the build-up to late March 1941, when Yugoslavia signed up to the Tripartite Pact, a coup followed, and the Croatian Peasant Party leader Vladko Maček joined the new government. According to the historian Darko Bekić, whom SABH quotes, the small Ustaša movement and a few hundred of its followers showed notable organisational readiness and a sense of political timing in those days. In Bjelovar they acted on 8 April, two days before units of Maček's Peasant Protection (Seljačka zaštita) entered the town, disarmed the royal army garrison and took power.

A second SABH article adds that the town's mayor, Julije Makanec, proclaimed the "resurrection" of the NDH there on 8 April, two days before Slavko Kvaternik did so officially in Zagreb. Makanec went on to become the state's minister of education.

The Bjelovar Ustaše soon showed what their rule would mean. Local Serbs were ordered to wear armbands marked "Srbin", which Boris Milošević of the Serb National Council later called a sign of what awaited them. Shootings and incidents followed in the town and the countryside, and the local authorities asked Zagreb for help. On 17 April Ante Pavelić issued a decree for the defence of the people and the state; two days later, SABH writes, a special order placed Serbs, Jews and Roma outside the law. Hundreds of Bjelovar Serbs were meanwhile held in the new Danica camp near Koprivnica, and most of them, in the second SABH account, later passed through Jadovno and Jasenovac.

The Ustaše offered a pretext for Gudovac. In the second SABH account, they pointed to the killing of several Croatian peasants near Bjelovar by soldiers of the defeated Yugoslav army who rejected the new state, and the article says that this did happen. Its author nevertheless calls the shooting of people who had no connection with those deaths a message to everyone the new authorities considered undesirable.

On the day itself, Eugen Dido Kvaternik, the NDH interior minister, arrived in Bjelovar and met local Ustaše. According to SABH, the killings in Gudovac followed an hour or two later. Novosti attributes the order itself to Kvaternik, and says about 80 members of Maček's Peasant Protection, now turned into an Ustaša unit, carried out the arrests. SABH names Martin Cikoš, commander of the Gudovac "protectors" and chairman of the municipal committee of the Peasant Party, as the leader, with Milan Pavlešić, Franjo Grivić, Dragutin Gosarić and Mijo Panić among the men who joined him. That naming comes from SABH's account alone.

Arrests began early in the morning in Gudovac itself, SABH writes, and continued after noon in the surrounding villages: Veliko and Malo Korenovo, Prgomelje, Bolč, Klokočevac, Tuk, Stančić and Breza. SABH puts the number held at the municipal building at about 200, among them three Orthodox priests. The same account counts 199 Serbs and one Croat among the 200 arrested. A second SABH piece gives a different picture of the arresting party, saying about 40 armed men entered Gudovac with orders to find all the Serb men and gather them in one place.

One of the survivors, Ilija Jarić of Veliko Korenovo, described his own arrest, quoted by Novosti. At about three in the afternoon, he said, 40 men came to the village and shouted that all Orthodox Christians must stay at home, adding that nothing would happen to them. They beat on the doors with rifle butts and ordered the men to raise their hands. Jarić said the villagers were herded into a farmyard, searched and listed by a man in the uniform of a Yugoslav lieutenant, who, to Jarić, looked like a peasant in borrowed officer's clothes. The man began writing down names but stopped after four. Guards were told to shoot anyone who ran, and no one was to speak or look at each other. About 32 men from the village were then driven to Gudovac, and on the way were made to sing Ustaša songs and shout "Long live Pavelić, long live Kvaternik".

The prisoners were led from the municipal building towards the river in a column four abreast, escorted, in SABH's first account, by about 80 armed men. On the muddy market meadow came the order to halt, then a volley. SABH says the executioners bayoneted the wounded afterwards, covered the bodies with lime and spread a thin layer of earth over them. Novosti also says the prisoners were shot and the bodies covered with lime, and puts the shooting at dusk.

The second SABH account differs on the method. It says the men were forced to lie on the ground and killed one after another by having their throats cut, then thrown into a large pit. The two accounts differ on the means of killing.

By Novosti's count, 195 people died on the spot; two wounded men were arrested and killed in hospital; and three survived by what the paper calls a miracle. SABH names the three as Ostoja Sekulić, Ilija Jarić and Milan Margetić. Novosti says one more survivor was saved, after lying at the execution site for two days.
content.h2: German officers and the killers' release
content.p: Novosti writes that two days later a German commission came to the site, ordered the bodies dug up and photographed, and counted 187 corpses. German soldiers briefly arrested the men who had carried out the shootings, took them to Bjelovar and held them in the town's grammar school, but they were soon released without consequences, according to Novosti.

SABH adds more about the German reaction. It says the German command assumed that atrocities of this kind would provoke armed resistance from the Serbs, who made up a quarter of the population of the NDH, and took over the town administration from the Ustaše. According to SABH, members of the Wehrmacht high command complained to Hitler that the Ustaše made their work harder with needless crimes, and, according to the memoirs of the senior German general in the NDH, Hitler answered that the Croats had suffered enough and should be allowed to let off steam. On 30 April an order stated that "cleansing" actions should take place under German army supervision, and the ringleaders of Gudovac were let out of prison. This exchange is reported on SABH's authority alone, from a memoir the article cites.

Novosti notes that doubts and rival lists about the number of dead from Gudovac still exist. The Bjelovar branch of the postwar veterans' association SUBNOR reached 196 victims in the late 1940s. Ilija Jarić compiled his own list and counted 201. Lazo Tesla and Branko Jurlina identified 192 names. Historians most often use the figure of the German commission, which recorded 187 dead when the bodies were exhumed. SABH's memorial text says 195, and the same figure appears in the Novosti description of the shooting.
content.h2: The monument and the fight over memory
content.p: After the war the victims were reburied near the village church and later moved back to the execution site, Novosti writes. SABH says a memorial ossuary for 195 Serb victims was built there in 1955 and extended in 1969. SABH names the sculptor Vojin Bakić's monument "Žrtva"; Novosti and the second SABH account call his monument there "Pred streljanje" ("Before the Firing Squad"), also known as "Gudovčan". Bakić was from Bjelovar; SABH records that his brother Milan, an antifascist leader in the town, and three other brothers were taken to the Jadovno camp in 1941 and killed there, while Vojin survived the war.

The monument and ossuary did not survive the 1990s. SABH says that during the last war the monument was levelled, the ossuary mined and the plaques smashed. A SABH author argues that after democracy returned, more than 3,000 antifascist monuments were destroyed, and criticises the early-1990s decision by Bjelovar's elected authorities to take a street from the Bakić brothers, as well as the move to name a street after Makanec. SABH says the site has since been tidied and the plaques with the victims' names restored. Novosti reports that the Serb National Council and the Bjelovar antifascist association had a memorial plaque restored, and that an initiative exists to bring back Bakić's monument or, failing that, to place another of his sculptures there.

On 28 April, Serb minority councils and antifascist groups gather at the site. At one commemoration, held under movement restrictions with about 20 people present, Boris Milošević of the Serb National Council told the gathering that strong forces in society deny the Gudovac killings in order to play down the criminal nature of the NDH. At the 82nd anniversary, attended by descendants and officials including Bjelovar's mayor Dario Hrebak, Vesna Teršelič of Documenta and the Anti-Fascist League said the occasion was a chance for cities to rename streets named after Ustaša officials. Hrebak spoke of a politician who the day before had shouted the Ustaša salute in the parliament.

VeDRA reprinted an article by the historian Hrvoje Klasić, who points to the massacre, committed only weeks after 10 April 1941, against revisionist claims that those killed in the NDH had been enemies of the new state. VeDRA introduces it as a somewhat forgotten massacre.
